HDR looks artificial: inspect local contrast, halos, saturation, and whether shadow lifting erased the scene’s dark adaptation cues. PHOTO-17
A stitched scene has doubled objects: check parallax, scene motion, exposure mismatch, and whether the camera pivoted around its center of projection. PHOTO-18
A documentary image’s meaning is unclear: recover caption, date, author, publication context, and whether the image was staged or altered. PHOTO-09 · PHOTO-14

Chapter.Content: These checks connect engineering to visual judgment. The goal is not to remove every defect. A flare streak, blur, grain, clipped highlight, long perspective, or rough composite can be part of the intended image. The goal is to know which physical or computational process produced it, so that the choice is deliberate and the claim made about the image is honest. PHOTO-04 · PHOTO-09 · PHOTO-11
Photograph as composition, not inventory

A camera frame is a bounded rectangle. The edges are active: they cut objects, create implied continuation, and determine whether the viewer sees a stable subject or an accidental crop. A horizon near the center can divide the image into equal fields; a high horizon emphasizes foreground texture, while a low horizon gives greater weight to sky. A diagonal line can move the eye through depth; a curve can lead it in a slower path. Repetition establishes rhythm, while a break in repetition becomes a point of emphasis. Symmetry can feel ceremonial or static; an offset subject can feel more dynamic if another form balances it. PHOTO-05 · PHOTO-16

Negative space is not unused image area. It separates forms, sets a subject’s scale, and can make direction or isolation legible. Simplifying a background can be achieved by moving the camera, changing focal length from a new position, opening aperture, waiting for the subject to move, or changing the light ratio. Each operation changes a different property. A shallow depth of field may dissolve a distracting background but also remove useful context. A high-contrast background may overpower the subject even when blurred. The photographer should decide whether the place is part of the story or merely competing detail. PHOTO-03 · PHOTO-05

Photography’s historical examples offer a way to practice this reading. Compare a documentary portrait that includes a worksite with a close crop of a worker’s face. The first frames labor and environment; the second emphasizes expression or identity. Compare an FSA image with the caption and without it; the same visual facts can point to a different cause or policy. Compare a staged composite to a single exposure; lighting, shadows, reflections, and perspective may be the clues that reveal construction, but the accompanying claim remains decisive. Visual analysis starts with what is present in the frame and then asks what evidence supports the story we infer. PHOTO-09 · PHOTO-14
Processes shape which events can be photographed

The earliest photographic processes make capture constraints concrete. Niépce’s bitumen-on-plate process required hours of exposure. The daguerreotype recorded a unique image on a polished, silvered plate; its appearance changes with viewing angle and it has no negative from which identical prints can be made. Talbot’s calotype used a paper negative to produce multiple positives, trading some fine detail for reproducibility. Wet-plate collodion later gave sharp, reproducible negatives but required the plate to be coated, exposed, and developed while wet, so photographers brought a portable darkroom into the field. Dry-plate gelatin emulsions could be prepared and stored before exposure, reducing the time pressure at the scene; roll film then made multiple exposures practical. Process choices changed not only image quality but which subjects, locations, and social practices were possible. PHOTO-02 · PHOTO-05 · PHOTO-14

A later extreme was the rapatronic camera for photographing nuclear detonations. Its Faraday shutter used a brief magnetic pulse to rotate the polarization of light passing through glass between polarizers. This opens an optical gate without mechanically moving a shutter blade. A participant’s MIT interview describes the coil-and-glass mechanism; the Smithsonian’s example records an exposure of one ten-millionth of a second, or 100 nanoseconds. Polarizers reject most light, but the technique makes an otherwise impossibly brief event recordable. It illustrates a recurring pattern in photography: a specialized capture system may sacrifice light, convenience, or normal color rendition to isolate a time interval ordinary shutters cannot reach. PHOTO-02

Dutch still-life painting offers a useful visual lesson for photographers. A highlight’s shape and movement can reveal the reflecting environment: windows appear as bright structured reflections in glass or polished metal, while a rough surface breaks them into broader patches. Vanitas still lifes use skulls, clocks, extinguished candles, and decaying food as symbols of mortality. When photographing a reflective object, change the shape and position of the source or reflector to control the highlight; a small bright spot often records the source geometry more clearly than the object’s color. These handout examples connect source geometry, material appearance and deliberate symbolism with photographic composition. PHOTO-11 · PHOTO-16
Motion and the mechanics of photography

An early shutter converted image making from long exposure toward action capture. Muybridge’s horse sequences used carefully timed shutters, trip wires, and multiple cameras; the image series answered a focused question about gait and made motion analyzable as samples. In the late nineteenth century, dry plates and roll film became more sensitive, increasing the need for reliable shutters. Leaf shutters open near the lens and can synchronize flash across much of their speed range; focal-plane shutters expose a traveling slit at high speeds, which can distort fast motion because different sensor rows see different moments. These designs are engineering compromises among speed, flash synchronization, cost, and geometric distortion. PHOTO-05 · PHOTO-09 · PHOTO-14

Light spectra and surface reflectance

Illumination can change the wavelengths a surface returns. Under a blue-heavy source, a red-looking object can appear dark because little energy arrives in the wavelengths its reflectance returns most strongly. This is why color appearance changes with illumination and why a three-number material color is a convenient approximation rather than a full spectral material model.

The spectral view also explains metamer failure. Suppose two reflectance functions give the same cone responses under illuminant . Under a different illuminant , the products and can yield different cone responses. A camera may also have response curves unlike the standard observer’s cones. Color management is therefore a chain of calibrated transforms, not a universal table of named colors. CMU-14

A final synthesis through four questions

When a renderer maps a texture onto a receding triangle, ask four questions. What is the representation? A surface point maps to texture coordinates. What is the continuous target? The average texture radiance over a pixel footprint. What is the discrete method? Perspective-correct coordinates, a mip level, and a reconstruction filter. What error remains? Aliasing, blur, or anisotropic distortion. This frames a visual artifact as a mismatch between target and approximation.

When a path tracer shows bright speckles, ask similarly. What quantity is estimated? A light-transport integral. What is the sampling density? Perhaps uniform over a hemisphere. Does it place samples where the contribution is large? If not, rare samples receive large weights and variance increases. What can be changed? Importance sampling, MIS, stratification, more samples, or a more robust path strategy. The image is noisy for a mathematical reason that can be named.

When an animated character’s hand misses a target, ask whether the forward transform chain is correct, whether the inverse-kinematics objective matches the desired pose, whether the Jacobian is conditioned, and whether joint constraints are encoded. When a mesh smooths into a smaller shape, ask which discrete Laplacian is used, which frequency modes it attenuates, and what feature constraints should remain. Across rendering, animation, and geometry, the useful sequence is representation, target, approximation, and error. It keeps the computation attached to the phenomenon it is meant to model.
Limits and a practical checklist
Before claiming a visual quantity has been recovered, ask:

Is the output local (a normal, edge, or flow vector) or global (a surface, object pose, or camera trajectory)? What integration or consistency step connects those levels?

A compact field workflow

ListItem.Content: Choose the viewpoint before the lens. Walk to the position that gives the intended foreground-background relations; then choose focal length and framing. Keep the viewpoint fixed if you want to compare focal lengths. PHOTO-01
Decide which motion may blur. Set a shutter time for the subject and camera stability. Stabilize the camera when it helps, but remember it cannot freeze a moving subject. PHOTO-01 · PHOTO-10

Choose aperture for depth of field, then evaluate diffraction. Focus on the plane that carries the most important detail. If deep focus is necessary, consider focus stacking or a different viewpoint rather than stopping down without limit. PHOTO-03 · PHOTO-04

Protect highlight information and collect enough photons. Use raw capture when later adjustment matters. Raise gain only after considering whether more exposure, aperture, lighting, or frame accumulation is possible. PHOTO-06 · PHOTO-08 · PHOTO-10

Read the light. Infer source size and direction from shadows, estimate the key-to-fill relation, and decide whether bounce, diffusion, a flag, or flash will help. Match flash color to ambient light if both appear in the frame. PHOTO-15 · PHOTO-16

Treat color as illumination plus reflectance plus rendering. Choose a neutral reference deliberately, preserve raw data if uncertain, and view through a known color space and display when accuracy matters. PHOTO-12 · PHOTO-13

Use computation where repeated measurements are compatible. Burst averaging suits stable scenes; exposure bracketing suits static high-range scenes; panorama stitching requires a common center of projection; each method needs alignment and artifact checks. PHOTO-10 · PHOTO-17 · PHOTO-18

Inspect the final viewing size. Depth of field, aliasing, sharpening, tone mapping, and color all depend on output scale and display context. A crop or enlargement can expose flaws that were invisible in a small preview. PHOTO-03 · PHOTO-07 · PHOTO-17

Chapter.Content: Putting the system together

The most useful habit is to move through the imaging chain in causal order. First identify the intended viewpoint and subject relation. Then decide which distances should be sharp and which motion should remain visible. Estimate the light, choose exposure controls, and leave headroom for important highlights. Consider whether the sensor is sampling enough detail and whether repeated captures can reduce noise or extend range. After capture, treat white balance, tone, denoising, sharpening, and compression as transformations with specific assumptions. Finally, inspect the result at its intended size and ask whether its visual claim matches its method.

For example, a night street portrait may need the photographer to move close enough to separate the subject from a lit storefront, but a very wide lens from that close position exaggerates facial perspective. A longer lens from farther back can preserve a more natural face, though the photographer must account for traffic and background. A fast shutter freezes expression; a large aperture admits light and softens the storefront; a nearby flash can lift the face but may create a hard shadow. Bouncing the flash from a wall or using a small diffuser changes its apparent source size. A warm gel can bring the flash closer to tungsten signage. Raw capture leaves room to balance the mixed sources, but the correct balance may preserve some warm color rather than neutralize every lamp. PHOTO-01 · PHOTO-03 · PHOTO-13 · PHOTO-16

A star photograph asks for different choices. A wide aperture gathers light, but lens aberration may distort stars near the frame edge. A longer exposure gathers more photons but stretches stars because Earth rotates. Tracking the sky counters that motion but blurs an untracked foreground; compositing tracked sky with a separate foreground image solves one geometric problem by introducing a composite and alignment problem. Stacking many short exposures reduces random noise but requires registration, rejection of satellites or hot pixels, and careful handling of moving clouds. Every technique is strongest when its assumptions are explicit. PHOTO-02 · PHOTO-04 · PHOTO-08 · PHOTO-09 · PHOTO-10

A landscape panorama adds yet another chain. The photographer selects a projection and pivot, captures sufficient overlap, avoids nearby motion, aligns features, estimates the transform, blends seams, crops to a meaningful field, and renders a perspective view suited to the display. More pixels alone do not guarantee a readable picture. A carefully framed wide image can be more expressive than an indiscriminate full rotation; conversely, a navigable spherical image may be the right record of a place even if no single flat crop can show it all. PHOTO-05 · PHOTO-18

These examples return to the course’s central idea: photography joins physical optics, computation, visual perception, artistic choices, and social meaning. The photographer is not a passive recorder and the processor is not a neutral afterthought. Good practice comes from knowing what each stage measures, what it assumes, and what it changes. That knowledge makes it possible to choose tradeoffs deliberately, to explain how an image was made, and to distinguish a useful transformation from a misleading one.
